transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-09-09
Start: 14:00 PDT
Duration: 75 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (AE, Redwood), Priya Malhotra (SE, Redwood), Marta Alvarez (CTO, HarborTech), Devon Pierce (Head of Infra), Sana Qureshi (Security Engineer), Liam O'Connor (Compliance Manager)

Auto-generated Summary: (may be incomplete)
  - Discussed KMS options and rotation policy
  - Walked through egress proxy and approved destination list
  - Mapped SOC2 evidence to current HarborTech controls

Transcript:
[00:00:00] Jordan Lee: Hey everyone, thanks for joining on a Friday — appreciate it. Quick roll call, then we'll jump into the K M S questions from your security team.
[00:00:12] Marta Alvarez: Hi, Marta here.
[00:00:14] Devon Pierce: Devon on my side.
[00:00:17] Sana Qureshi: Sana, Security.
[00:00:19] Liam O'Connor: Liam, Compliance.
[00:00:22] Priya Malhotra: And I'm Priya from Redwood, I'll take the deep network bits.
[00:00:28] Jordan Lee: Cool. Agenda is KMS/HSM, ingress/egress patterns for Private, audit logs, and then SOC2 evidence mapping. We'll try to leave 10 minutes for questions.
[00:00:40] Marta Alvarez: Sounds good. Our primary ask: we need to ensure keys never leave our control and we need a clear rotation policy and tamper evidence.
[00:00:51] Priya Malhotra: Totally. You have three general options with our Private offering: integrate your cloud K M S (e.g., GCP KMS or AWS KMS), bring your own HSM via KMIP or an HSM-backed gateway, or use Redwood's managed HSM — which we can deploy in your VPC and provide attestation. Note, "Redwood Privet" (sic) managed HSM has a slightly different SL and contract.
[00:01:14] Devon Pierce: Quick question — if we use our cloud K M S, does the key ever land on the inference hosts? We run a strict no-plaintext-key rule.
[00:01:24] Priya Malhotra: No plaintext keys. The runtime will fetch wrapped key material and use a K V cache for session encryption; the private key operations stay inside the HSM or cloud K M S. We do, uh, maintain per-instance ephemeral wrapping keys but those are memory-only and never persisted.
[00:01:44] Sana Qureshi: When you say "KV cache" some of our docs show "K V cash" being logged — we've seen weird transcriptions in older notes, but the security property matters.
[00:01:52] Priya Malhotra: Right, sorry for the transcription quirks. It's an in-memory K V cache (key-value cache) for ephemeral tokenization contexts, not long-term secrets storage.
[00:02:06] Liam O'Connor: For SOC2 we need evidence of key rotation and access logs to key ops. Can you feed key operation logs into our SIEM?
[00:02:16] Jordan Lee: Yes — we can stream audit events for KMS ops to an S3-compatible endpoint or directly to your Splunk/Datadog via secure forwarder. The event payload includes requestor principal, operation, timestamp, and the HSM attestation ID.
[00:02:34] Marta Alvarez: About data residency: we have EU-only data for some customers. Can we guarantee that inference never routes to non-EU regions?
[00:02:43] Priya Malhotra: With Private you control the VPC — so routing stays in-region. We also support route policies to pin inference traffic to specific pools. If you want absolute proof we can provide network egress logs and signed attestations for the region.
[00:02:59] Devon Pierce: Let's talk egress: our policy permits only specific outbound destinations — update servers, package mirrors, and our approved telemetry collectors. How does Redwood handle external calls or model updates?
[00:03:12] Priya Malhotra: By default, Private has a locked-down egress policy. Model downloads are allowed only from configured artifact repositories (you can host an internal S3 or use our mirrored artifact repository inside your VPC). Runtime can call back to Redwood control plane only over mutually TLS-auth'd endpoints if you opted for a paired-control-plane mode; otherwise control plane traffic is via a customer-controlled egress proxy.
[00:03:35] Jordan Lee: To add, many customers put an egress proxy (squid or nginx) with an allowlist. We recommend TLS interception is off — instead use mTLS and client certs for authentication and an application-level allowlist.
[00:03:48] Sana Qureshi: Do you support DNS allowlisting? We prefer deny-all plus explicit FQDNs and don't want dynamic DNS to undermine it.
[00:03:56] Priya Malhotra: Yep. We support both IP and FQDN allowlists. We also ship a small sidecar that does DNS resolution checks and tags flows for audit. Caution: FQDN allowlists can be spoofed with CNAME chains so we advise TTL and CNAME resolution checks.
[00:04:15] Liam O'Connor: For audit logs retention — SOC wants 12 months online and 7 years archived for some control sets. What's feasible?
[00:04:25] Jordan Lee: We can push logs to your long term storage; we don't force retention limits. For online searches we keep 90 days indexed by default, then move to cold storage on your S3 for longer terms.
[00:04:37] Marta Alvarez: On RBAC and SSO — we use Okta with SCIM. We need per-operator roles that can manage deployments but not access inference payloads.
[00:04:47] Priya Malhotra: Our Private control plane supports SAML SSO with SCIM and granular RBAC. We have built-in roles (admin, infra-operator, audit-reader) and you can define custom roles. Operator accounts can be scoped away from request-level logs — we can redact user payloads from operational logs.
[00:05:05] Devon Pierce: Does Redwood require inbound openings into our private network? We want strictly outbound-only and no inbound holes.
[00:05:13] Priya Malhotra: You can run in an outbound-only model. The control plane can be polled outbound by an agent, or you can deploy a webhook forwarder inside the VPC that retrieves updates from a pull endpoint. No inbound NAT is required.
[00:05:27] Jordan Lee: Quick pause — are there particular gaps from your SOC2 readiness doc you want to walk through?
[00:05:33] Liam O'Connor: Yes: we flagged lack of documented key ceremonies, unclear separation of duties for infra ops, and incomplete log integrity proofs.
[00:05:43] Priya Malhotra: For key ceremonies we can provide a documented process for rotation including KMS rotation API calls, HSM admin rotations, and staff steps. Separation of duties: we recommend a two-person approval for key material changes and keep those actions in an immutable audit ledger (signed events).
[00:05:58] Sana Qureshi: On log integrity — can logs be signed at source? We want non-repudiation; if someone tampers with a host we need evidence.
[00:06:07] Priya Malhotra: Yes — the agent can sign log bundles with a host key, and that signature can be verified against an archived root of trust. We can also ship logs to a WORM bucket or append-only ledger.
[00:06:20] Devon Pierce: Network-level controls: we use strict IPTABLES baseline and eBPF observability. Any recommended firewall rules?
[00:06:29] Priya Malhotra: We'll share a minimal iptables baseline in the runbook: deny by default, allow loopback, allow VPC-internal control-plane ports, allow egress to approved artifact repos and telemetry. Also recommend node-level egress via a single NAT gateway with source-ip rewrite so egress auditing is simpler.
[00:06:48] Jordan Lee: Also consider a dedicated egress proxy with mTLS and client certs — that centralizes allowlisting and makes L7 control easier.
[00:06:55] Marta Alvarez: For the pilot we want to test model download integrity and runtime performance — need to prove no data skews to other tenants.
[00:07:05] Priya Malhotra: For model integrity we provide signed model artifacts with SHA-256 and an optional provenance manifest. For tenancy isolation the runtime uses per-tenant namespaces and enforced KV cache partitioning so cross-tenant leakage is mitigated.
[00:07:22] Liam O'Connor: Does Redwood provide SOC2 evidence for the managed components if we elect Redwood-managed HSM inside our VPC?
[00:07:30] Jordan Lee: We can provide Redwood's SOC2 Type II report for the managed control plane and a separate attestation for HSM appliance deployments. But for HSMs physically in your VPC, some responsibilities remain with you and we'll document the shared responsibility matrix.
[00:07:46] Devon Pierce: Any thoughts on TLS interception by our proxy for outbound egress? We normally avoid MITM for consumer privacy reasons.
[00:07:54] Priya Malhotra: We recommend avoiding TLS intercept. Use mTLS and certificate pinning for control traffic. For package mirrors you can host an internal mirror and serve over HTTPS with certs you control.
[00:08:09] Sana Qureshi: Can we restrict access so that only our SIEM service can pull logs, not someone in Redwood or third parties?
[00:08:16] Jordan Lee: Absolutely. We can configure exporter endpoints to only accept connections from your SIEM IPs and rotate exporter credentials. Logs routed to your buckets are under your IAM policies.
[00:08:29] Marta Alvarez: Ok let's move into the SOC2 evidence mapping slide — (screen share) — we listed controls where Redwood interacts: CC6, CC7, CC8...
[00:08:40] Jordan Lee: For CC6 (logical and physical access) we can provide access rosters, SSO audit trails, and console login events. For CC7 (system operations) we can give runbooks, deployment logs, and automated test results.
[00:08:56] Liam O'Connor: We need to see proof for change management and emergency patches too.
[00:09:02] Priya Malhotra: We keep an immutable deployment changelog and can show artifacts for a sample time window. Emergency patches are tagged with reason codes and require two approvers in the workflow.
[00:09:14] Devon Pierce: Back to egress — what about model telemetry? Can we opt out of telemetry entirely?
[00:09:21] Jordan Lee: Yes. Telemetry is optional. You can opt out or route telemetry to your collector only. If you route to us for feature telemetry, we can do an IP-limited endpoint.
[00:09:33] Sana Qureshi: One more: how do you handle secrets in CI/CD for deploying models — we rotate deploy keys frequently and can't have long-lived tokens baked in.
[00:09:44] Priya Malhotra: We recommend short-lived artifact tokens and a deploy-time agent that pulls via signed URLs. If you prefer, we support a signed-token exchange using your KMS so no long-lived tokens are required.
[00:09:58] Jordan Lee: (pause) — wrapping up technical: Priya will share the iptables baseline and the egress runbook. I'll share SOC2 package and our KMS whitepaper. Sana will provide data residency specifics.
[00:10:12] Marta Alvarez: Sounds good. A few off-script items — what's the fallback if your dedicated node is saturated and we have no burst capacity?
[00:10:21] Priya Malhotra: We support a few fallback modes: prioritized request routing to a lower-capacity model variant, or routing to an on-prem cold pool. For hard SLOs you should provision reserved capacity. We'll document the modes in the runbook.
[00:10:36] Devon Pierce: For the pilot can we schedule a dedicated two-node pool with metrics collection (latency percentiles, token counts, egress flows)?
[00:10:45] Jordan Lee: Yes — we'll provision that as a pilot. We'll also enable transparent tracing so we can correlate model requests to egress logs for the audit.
[00:10:54] Liam O'Connor: Any competitors you think do this better?
[00:10:57] Jordan Lee: A few folks do parts of this; CloudLLM has a similar hosted offering but weaker private-network features, SelfHostLabs is more DIY. We focus on combining runtime performance with enterprise controls.
[00:11:12] Sana Qureshi: Quick nit — what's the plan for key revocation if a node is compromised?
[00:11:18] Priya Malhotra: Revoke at KMS level, force key rotation, and revoke any node certificates via cert revocation list; we also present tamper-evident log slices to show timeline.
[00:11:30] Marta Alvarez: Okay, that's helpful. Let's list follow-ups — can you put the recommended firewall snippets in a gist? That helps our infra team.
[00:11:38] Priya Malhotra: Yep will do. We'll include iptables and nft examples, plus a managed egress proxy config.
[00:11:46] Jordan Lee: Great. Any final questions before we close?
[00:11:50] Devon Pierce: Nothing else from infra.
[00:11:53] Sana Qureshi: No, thanks.
[00:11:55] Liam O'Connor: No, thanks — scheduling note: we'd like the SOC2 artifacts by early next week.
[00:12:03] Jordan Lee: We'll aim for Friday delivery for SOC2 artifacts. Priya will get the runbook by Monday.
[00:12:10] Marta Alvarez: Good, thanks everyone.
[00:12:13] Jordan Lee: Thanks all — talk soon.
